chapterGroups.title: Theme Gallery
description: Fifteen chapters, one per shipped theme. Click them in the sidebar and the canvas changes
colour -- no command, no setting to find first.
Every chapter below names a theme of its own in the 'theme' field beside its title, and every
chapter has the same six quests in the same six positions. That is the whole design and it is
deliberate rather than lazy: if the chapters differed in layout as well as in colour, a
difference you saw while clicking between them could be either, and an exhibit that varies two
things shows nothing.
What a chapter's theme covers is the canvas and the quest overlay -- the graph, its nodes,
their rings and connectors, the backdrop, and the panel you get when you open a quest. What it
does NOT cover is the frame around them: the sidebar, the header, the title, the buttons and
the tooltips are drawn in YOUR theme, whatever chapter you are standing in. So opening a
violet chapter shows a violet canvas inside an otherwise unchanged book, and both are visible
at once.
That split is why the theme row at the foot of the sidebar never fights with the chapter. Your
choice is the book; the chapter's is its own picture. Clicking the theme row changes the
frame, the buttons and the other chapters, and leaves the canvas you are looking at alone.
The motion row is yours as well, and it wins over any theme: a theme sets how long its
transitions last and what curve they use, so Vanilla Plus and High Contrast have a motion of
zero and snap, but turning motion off overrides even an animated theme. That precedence is
deliberate -- a reskin must not be able to re-enable animation for somebody who cannot
comfortably use it.
Corners are the one part of a theme you cannot see yet from this file alone: the radius is
read and applied, and it rounds the panels and controls built on Armature, but the quest book
draws its own rectangles squarely. Two themes below carry a radius of 8 and two carry 0, which
is where that difference would show.
The shipped themes, in the order the sidebar's theme row cycles them: Modern, Tome, Vanilla
Plus, High Contrast, Monochrome, Paper, Obsidian, Amethyst, Copper, Redstone, Nether, End,
Deep Dark, Terminal, Neon.

chapters.title: Modern
chapters.subtitle: The theme a client starts with
description: The appearance this project has shipped with, and the one every screenshot before themes
were themeable was taken in. Nothing in this chapter is new.
It is the baseline the other fourteen are read against, and it is also the one theme that
states all forty-one of its colours rather than inheriting any -- so what you see here is
what every other theme starts from.
Look at the node borders: an available node's ring is the same colour as the word
'available' beside a quest, and a locked node's outline is deliberately dimmer than the
word 'blocked'. Those became separate values this round, and both of those relationships
are asserted rather than incidental.
Close the book while standing here and nothing changes: the canvas IS your theme, because
this is the theme you started with.

quests.title: The Yard
quests.subtitle: The entry node, and the only one named
description: Four things are on screen at once when this chapter opens, which is why it is first:
an available node, a locked one, a connector line between them, and a hover ring as
soon as you put the pointer on this one.
The hover ring follows the node's shape. On a circle it is a ring -- it used to be a
rectangle drawn around a disc, which reads as two unrelated things stacked.

quests.title: The Furnace
quests.subtitle: A count, so the progress bar appears
description: Three ingots, so this is the row that draws a progress bar -- a recessed track and a
state-coloured fill, which is two of the theme's surfaces in six pixels of height.
Carry some of the eight and open this quest: the bar is part of the way across and the
count beside it reads in the faint text tone. It is the smallest place a theme can be
wrong and still look fine everywhere else.

quests.title: The Line
quests.subtitle: Repeatable, with a cooldown
description: A hexagon at size 40 with the icon at 0.6 of its box, so this is visibly a minor job
rather than a milestone -- and a repeatable one, which is why its border never takes
the completed colour and stays there.
The hexagon's taper is a straight line rather than an arc. That is what makes it a
hexagon and not a rounded rectangle, and at 40 pixels the two are easy to mistake for
each other.

quests.title: The Drive
quests.subtitle: An OR-gate, one optional task, and no rewards
description: Either of the two above will do -- minRequired is 1 -- so this unlocks the moment one
of them is finished and stays locked while both are not. That is what makes it the node
to watch for the locked wash and its dimmed icon.
The wash is a translucent black over the icon rather than a chip with a cross in the
corner. The chip used to sit in this node's bottom-right and read as a square pasted
over the artwork, hiding the one thing a node is on the canvas to show.
The checkmark is optional, so its row carries both tags at once: 'hand in' in the
available colour and 'optional' in faint, right-aligned, in one row.

tasks.title: I looked at the locked node

quests.title: The Inspection
quests.subtitle: Two hand-ins, in order, and a long description
description: Two checkmarks and sequentialTasks, so Submit starts on the first and moves down to
the second once the first is handed in. Both rows carry the 'hand in' tag in the
available colour for as long as they are undone.
This chapter's long description is here for one reason, and it is not the writing.
The overlay is a fixed header, a scrolling body and a fixed footer. The body clips, the
scrollbar appears when the content is taller than the clip, and the scrollbar's track
and its thumb are two colours that only exist when there is something to scroll.
Without a description this long none of it is ever drawn, which is how it went
unnoticed for a whole round. The scrollbar is also the newest pair of tokens in the
theme: it used to be drawn from the raised surface and a control edge, neither of which
was chosen for the job, so every theme got the same weak contrast between a track and
the panel behind it.
Scroll to the bottom and REQUIRES is there: two rows, each a tick or a cross in the
completed or blocked colour, naming the two quests above.
None of this needs doing beyond pressing two buttons, which is the honest shape of an
inspection.

tasks.title: And I have looked at the drive

quests.title: The Office
quests.subtitle: Invisible until it is done
description: You cannot see this node until it is complete, so there is a gap here and the gap
stays. A hidden node that left no hole would tell you exactly where it was.
The smallest node in the chapter at size 36 with the icon at 0.9 -- the other end of
the range from the railway, because an office should look crammed into the thing
holding it.

chapters.title: Tome
chapters.subtitle: Parchment and brass
description: A parchment and brass reskin, and the theme that proves a palette is a parameter rather
than a set of constants -- because two of its values differ from Modern's by more than a
tint.
Its selected ring is brass, not blue. A parchment canvas with a bright blue selection ring
is two palettes arguing, and that is the kind of thing only a second theme finds: a colour
that looked fine on its own turns out to have been chosen against the surfaces around it.
Its corner radius is 8 against Modern's 4, so it is the theme that makes the radius a real
parameter. Watch the quest overlay's panel and the buttons on it when you open a quest
here -- those are drawn through Armature and do round. The canvas underneath them does
not.

quests.title: Pens and Ink
quests.subtitle: The entry node, and the only one named
description: Same position, same shape, same size as The Yard -- and a different colour everywhere a
colour is used. That is the comparison this chapter exists to make.
The heading tones are the ones to look at. TASKS and REWARDS are drawn in a colour of
their own rather than in the body tone, and on a parchment palette that distinction is
carried by brightness rather than by hue.

quests.title: Bind It Shut
quests.subtitle: A count, so the progress bar appears
description: The bar here is drawn in brass rather than in the available-blue, because the bar takes
the state colour and the state colours are per-theme.
A theme that got its surfaces right and its state colours wrong shows up first on a
partly-filled bar and almost nowhere else.

quests.title: Copy the Page
quests.subtitle: Repeatable, with a cooldown
description: A hexagon at size 40, and it is the same shape arithmetic as in every other chapter --
Armature's span tables -- seen through a different theme.
Worth checking that the taper still reads on a warm background. A shape's silhouette is
not theme-dependent, but how visible it is very much is.

quests.title: The Catalogue
quests.subtitle: An OR-gate, one optional task, and no rewards
description: The locked node, while both of the two above are undone. Its wash is warmer here than
Modern's and its outline is darker, and neither was chosen separately: a locked node is
the panel colour dimmed, and the panel colour is the theme's.
The optional checkmark carries both tags in one row, as in every other chapter.

quests.title: First Reading
quests.subtitle: Two hand-ins, in order, and a long description
description: The long-description quest, as in every chapter, so the scrollbar appears here too --
and it does, in this theme's recessed surface and thumb colours, which are the two
tokens added this round.
Scroll down: REQUIRES is at the bottom with its tick and its cross. The cross is the
blocked tone, which recedes rather than turning red. Nothing has gone wrong; a
prerequisite simply is not met.
Two checkmarks with sequentialTasks, so Submit starts on the first and moves down. A
row of a body is washed with the row-hover colour, scaled by an eased amount, and
narrowed to the row's own content rather than to its box. A row of a stack stretches to
the full width of the body, so washing its box drew a highlight straight across the
whole panel. That was a real bug, and a screenshot found it rather than a test.
Its motion is the same 140ms on the same curve as Modern's, and that is on purpose: if
Tome also animated differently, a difference you saw while switching chapters could be
either one, and an exhibit that shows two variables shows nothing.
This paragraph, like its counterparts in the other fourteen chapters, exists to make
the body taller than the clip. If the scrollbar ever stops appearing, one of these got
shorter and everything it was demonstrating went with it.

tasks.title: And I have read to the end

quests.title: The Vault
quests.subtitle: Invisible until it is done
description: Hidden, like every chapter's last node, and in the same place -- so once you have
completed one gallery chapter you know exactly where the gap is.

chapters.title: Vanilla Plus
chapters.subtitle: Grey, square and still
description: Vanilla's own greys, tidied -- for a player who does not want their game restyled. It
catches two implementation mistakes at once, because two of its values are zero.
Motion is zero, and that is a difference you feel rather than see: click another chapter in
the sidebar and the canvas changes on the frame you click, where every other theme eases
over at least 60ms. Vanilla has no UI animation, so neither does this -- which only works
because a duration of zero means 'instant' rather than 'unset'. An earlier version read
zero as 'no opinion' and used the built-in duration, so this theme silently animated like
Modern while claiming not to.
Radius is zero, which is what 'looks like Minecraft' means, and it is the case a radius
implementation with a minimum of one gets wrong -- a theme cannot express 'square' if the
code has decided a corner is at least a pixel.
Note that the motion row in the sidebar still says what you set it to. A theme supplies
the default duration; your own switch, if you have turned motion off, wins over every
theme including the animated ones.

quests.title: Break the Ground
quests.subtitle: The entry node, and the only one named
description: Move the pointer onto this node and the ring arrives on the frame it is hovered. That
is the whole difference a zero motion makes, and this chapter and High Contrast are the
only two that show it.
The ring follows the shape, as everywhere: on a circle it is a ring rather than a
rectangle drawn around a disc.

quests.title: A Source
quests.subtitle: A count, so the progress bar appears
description: One bucket, so the count reads 0 / 1 until you have it and the bar has two pixels of
fill at most -- its own small test of the bar's minimum width.
The greys here are very close together, and that is the one place this theme is
unfriendly. Vanilla's palette is a narrow one, and four surfaces drawn from it have
less room between them than any other theme's.

quests.title: Plant Again
quests.subtitle: Repeatable, with a cooldown
description: A hexagon on a grey palette at the same size as every other chapter's. The state
colours here are still four distinguishable values even though every surface around
them is grey, and that is the thing a palette has to get right before anything else.

quests.title: Keep the Animals
quests.subtitle: An OR-gate, one optional task, and no rewards
description: Locked while both of the two above are undone. The dimmed icon on this theme is a flat
black, because vanilla's own dim is black -- so the item stays readable underneath it
rather than being hidden, which is the difference between a wash and a chip with a
cross drawn in the corner.

quests.title: Market Day
quests.subtitle: Two hand-ins, in order, and a long description
description: The scrollbar again, in this theme's track and thumb. Motion being zero has no effect
on it: scrolling is not animated in any theme, because the scroll is the pointer's own
gesture and easing it would put the content behind the finger.
Two sequential checkmarks, so Submit starts on the first and moves down once it is
handed in. Pressing it here is more useful than on the animated themes for one reason:
the held state snaps in every theme, because a press has to be immediate, so the only
visible difference is how the hover got there.
Scroll to the bottom for REQUIRES. Its tick is green and its cross is grey, and on a
greyscale palette the green is the only saturated thing in the body.
This paragraph, like its counterparts in the other fourteen chapters, exists to make
the body taller than the clip -- so the scrollbar's track and thumb are seen in all
fifteen palettes rather than in whichever chapter you happened to open first.
One thing to notice on this chapter that the others cannot show you: the paper surface
is barely lighter than the panel behind it, so the recessed areas and the raised strips
have almost no contrast to separate them. That is a real property of vanilla's palette
rather than a mistake in this theme, and it is why a light theme like Paper needs a
different relationship between its surfaces rather than a lighter version of the same
one.

quests.title: The Barn
quests.subtitle: Invisible until it is done
description: The third hidden node, in the third chapter, at the same position as every chapter's.
Everything in this file is arranged so that two chapters can be compared by clicking
between them without the layout moving underneath you. If a difference appears, it is
the theme. If the nodes jump, something is wrong with the file rather than the
renderer.

chapters.title: High Contrast
chapters.subtitle: Maximum legibility, no motion
description: Chosen to solve a problem rather than to look like somewhere: surfaces pushed to near
black, text to pure white, and every state a bright primary with no muddiness in it.
The two things that are washes in every other theme are much more opaque here. The
locked-node dimming and the row-hover highlight are the information you need to know
where a click will land, so a subtle hint is the wrong answer for this theme.
Motion is zero, as on Vanilla Plus, so nothing eases. Panels are square.
The panel borders are pure white, which is the loudest thing any shipped theme does and is
the point. If there is anywhere in the interface that draws a frame from a colour it
happens to have rather than from the border token, this is the chapter that shows it.

quests.title: First Step
quests.subtitle: The entry node, and the only one named
description: A white-on-black outline with a white title over it. The ring on hover is pure white
at full alpha, so it does not fade in at all -- hover and it appears.
Everything on this canvas is one of four unmissable colours, and that is the whole
design.

quests.title: Stock Up
quests.subtitle: A count, so the progress bar appears
description: The bar's track is pure black with a white border, and its fill is the state colour --
so a partially-filled bar is the clearest thing on this screen.
Hand in two and notice the count beside it: pure white, at the same weight as the label,
because this theme has no faint tone that is genuinely faint.

quests.title: Keep Going
quests.subtitle: Repeatable, with a cooldown
description: A white hexagon on black, at size 40, with the icon at 0.6 -- the sharpest a shape gets
in any of the fifteen chapters, because the border is a full-white outline two pixels
wide against nothing.

quests.title: Either Will Do
quests.subtitle: An OR-gate, one optional task, and no rewards
description: Locked, and deliberately so -- this is the node where the dimming wash matters most.
On this theme the wash is four-fifths opaque black rather than a hint, because 'this
node is not available' is the single most useful fact on the canvas if you cannot read
subtle contrast.
The icon is still visible under it, which is the line a wash has to walk: hide the
item entirely and the node stops being recognisable.

quests.title: Read This
quests.subtitle: Two hand-ins, in order, and a long description
description: The long-description quest, and the one where the overlay's typography is doing real
work: pure white on pure black, with the section headings in white as well rather than
in a dimmer tone.
That last part is the trade this theme makes and it is worth knowing about. TASKS and
REWARDS are ordinarily quieter than the body text, which makes a long page scannable.
Here they are not quieter, because a quieter heading is exactly what somebody using
this theme has said they cannot read -- so the sections are separated by a white rule
instead, and the page reads as a list of headings rather than as prose.
Scroll down for REQUIRES: its cross is a light grey rather than the usual dim one, so
an unmet prerequisite is legible without being alarming. Nothing has gone wrong when
you see it.
The scrollbar is white on black here, which makes it the most visible one in the whole
gallery. Compare it with Paper's, where the same two tokens have to do the opposite
job.
As in every other chapter this paragraph exists to make the body taller than the clip,
so the scrollbar is drawn in this palette rather than in whichever chapter you opened
first. Fifteen chapters, fifteen of these.

tasks.title: And I have read the footer

quests.title: The Last One
quests.subtitle: Invisible until it is done
description: Hidden, in the position every chapter's last node occupies, so the gap is where you
expect it.

chapters.title: Monochrome
chapters.subtitle: No hue anywhere, on purpose
description: Greys only. Not one of the forty-one colours in this theme has a hue, and that makes it a
test as much as a theme: every state here is a distinct brightness and nothing else, so
anywhere the interface leans on hue to tell available from complete is somewhere this
chapter is unreadable.
The four states are chosen far apart on purpose -- available at 210, in progress at 150,
complete at 255, blocked at 90 -- so the difference is unmistakable when you look for it
and invisible when you do not.
Building this theme found a real bug, which is worth recording because it is the kind
only a theme can find. The washes -- the dim over the world, the recessed surfaces, the
label backdrops -- started out inherited from Modern, on the reasonable-sounding grounds
that a wash is only a wash. Modern's are all a very slightly blue near-black, so the
no-hue-anywhere theme had five faintly tinted surfaces in it and nothing on screen would
ever have said so. A test that checks every token rather than the interesting ones caught
it, then caught a sixth one on the next run.

quests.title: Begin
quests.subtitle: The entry node, and the only one named
description: An available node here is a light grey, and the ring on hover is the brightest white
in the theme. Every distinction on this canvas is one of brightness.
Look at the connector line to the node above: it is a mid grey, which is brighter than
the blocked outline and dimmer than the available one. Those three values have to sit
in the right order for this theme to work at all.

quests.title: Gather
quests.subtitle: A count, so the progress bar appears
description: The bar's fill is the available grey and its track is a darker one, with no hue between
them to help. Four pixels of fill at the left edge is a real test of whether the two
greys are far enough apart.

quests.title: Again
quests.subtitle: Repeatable, with a cooldown
description: A hexagon, size 40. A shape's outline on a grey palette has nothing but a one-step
brightness change to distinguish itself from the canvas behind it, and the taper is
where that either works or does not.

quests.title: Blocked
quests.subtitle: An OR-gate, one optional task, and no rewards
description: The locked node, and this is the state that proves the theme is doing what it claims.
A locked node's outline is a mid-dark grey; the word 'blocked' beside a quest is a
lighter one. Both are grey, both are legible, and the difference between them is the
whole point.
In every one of the fifteen shipped themes those two values differ, and 'blocked' is
always the brighter of the pair -- a node you cannot click should recede, and the word
explaining why should not.

quests.title: Read
quests.subtitle: Two hand-ins, in order, and a long description
description: The long-description quest. On a theme with no hue anywhere, TASKS and REWARDS have
to be separated from the body text by brightness alone -- which is why the heading
tone here is nearly the same as the title tone, and why it works anyway.
This is the page to read if you want to know whether a greyscale interface is usable
or merely tidy. Scroll down and the REQUIRES cross appears in a darker grey than the
tick above it, with no colour to help.
The scrollbar's thumb is a light grey on a near-black track. It is the second-loudest
scrollbar in the gallery after High Contrast's, and the two are worth comparing
because they arrive at a similar contrast from opposite directions -- one by going to
pure white, the other by having nothing else to go to.
As in every chapter, this paragraph exists to make the body taller than the clip, so
the scrollbar is drawn in this palette rather than in whichever chapter you opened
first.

quests.title: Finished
quests.subtitle: Invisible until it is done
description: Hidden, in the same place as every chapter's last node.

chapters.title: Paper
chapters.subtitle: The only light theme there is
description: Dark ink on pale surfaces, and the only theme in the set that inverts the relationship
every other one assumes -- text is darker than the surface behind it.
That makes it worth opening even if you would never use it. Anywhere the interface
assumes 'brighter means more important', or draws a dark shadow, or uses white for a
highlight, this chapter makes it visible. A gallery of fourteen dark themes cannot find
those, because in all of them the assumption happens to be true.
Its dim is a pale haze rather than a dark one, which is the one place a light theme has
to make a real decision. The dim exists to push the world back behind the panel; a light
theme can do that with brightness as well as with darkness, and a light theme that dimmed
to black would be a pale panel on a black void, which reads as a bug.
Watch the locked node here in particular. Its wash is a translucent pale grey, which is
the opposite of what a dark theme does -- and the icon has to stay readable under it
either way.

quests.title: A Clean Page
quests.subtitle: The entry node, and the only one named
description: Dark ink on a pale canvas, which is the first thing you will notice and the only thing
that matters about this chapter.
The hover ring is near-black at half alpha. On every other theme the ring is a light
colour brightening; here it is a dark one appearing, and the two read surprisingly
differently.

quests.title: Three Sheets
quests.subtitle: A count, so the progress bar appears
description: The bar's track is a pale grey and its fill is a deep blue -- so on this theme the
filled part is the dark part, which is the reverse of every other chapter.
A theme that got its surfaces inverted and forgot the state colours would show up here
first, and almost nowhere else.

quests.title: Copy It Out
quests.subtitle: Repeatable, with a cooldown
description: A hexagon at size 40 on a pale canvas. Its outline is a mid-brown, which is the
closest thing this theme has to a border colour, and the taper holds up better here
than on the dark themes because a dark line on a light field is how ink works.

quests.title: Under Seal
quests.subtitle: An OR-gate, one optional task, and no rewards
description: This is the locked node, and it is the most interesting one in the gallery to look at
on this theme -- because the wash over a locked icon is a pale haze here rather than a
dark one.
The icon underneath is FADED rather than darkened. On a dark theme a lock dims the
item; on this one it washes it out. Both say 'not yet' and they arrive at it from
opposite directions, which is exactly the kind of thing a theme is allowed to decide.

quests.title: The Long Chapter
quests.subtitle: Two hand-ins, in order, and a long description
description: The long-description quest, and on this theme it is the most readable page in the
gallery -- which is a real property of a light theme rather than a preference. Body
text at this size, in a dark ink on a pale field, is the configuration that has been
measured most often and it shows.
Scroll down: the REQUIRES cross is a muted brown rather than a grey, because a pure
grey on a warm pale field looks like a printing error rather than a state.
The scrollbar here is the one to compare against High Contrast's. Both have to be
unmistakable, and they get there by opposite routes: white on black, and a deep brown
on cream. That is the whole argument for the scrollbar having tokens of its own rather
than borrowing the raised surface and a control edge, which is what it did before this
round.
As in every chapter, this paragraph exists to make the body taller than the clip, so
the scrollbar appears and is drawn in this palette.
One more thing worth noticing while you are here: the tooltip that follows the pointer
over a control on the sidebar is drawn in YOUR theme, not in this one. The chapter's
palette covers the canvas and this overlay, and nothing outside them -- so a pale
canvas can sit inside a dark frame without either looking broken.

quests.title: The Last Page
quests.subtitle: Invisible until it is done
description: Hidden, in the position every chapter's last node occupies.

chapters.title: Obsidian
chapters.subtitle: Near-black purple, lit from inside
description: Obsidian and crying obsidian: the darkest surfaces in the gallery, with a violet glow
doing all the work. Every colour here that is not near-black is a purple.
The interesting value is the connector line. On a canvas this dark a line has to be
brighter than the surface it crosses and dimmer than the nodes at either end, or the
graph reads as unconnected boxes -- and there is very little room between those two
constraints when the surface is at 11,9,20.
Radius is 2, so this is one of the two squarest themes. Compare the quest overlay's
panel against Tome's while you are here: the same panel, drawn through the same code,
and the corners are the only difference.

quests.title: Into the Dark
quests.subtitle: The entry node, and the only one named
description: A violet glow on nearly-black purple. The available colour here is the brightest
violet in the theme, and the completed colour is a paler one that only appears once
you have finished something.
The hover ring is a pale lavender at half alpha, which against this canvas is a
visible glow rather than a highlight.

quests.title: Four Blocks
quests.subtitle: A count, so the progress bar appears
description: The bar's track is a recessed near-black and its fill is the state violet, so on this
canvas the fill is the only light thing in the row.
This is the theme where a partially-filled bar is most legible and a fully-empty one
is least -- an empty track at this darkness is nearly invisible, which is a deliberate
trade rather than an oversight: an empty bar is not information.

quests.title: Mine Again
quests.subtitle: Repeatable, with a cooldown
description: A hexagon at size 40 in violet outline on near-black. The straight taper of a hexagon
reads as a thinner line than a circle's arc at the same weight, so a shape drawn in a
dark theme looks sharper than the same shape drawn in a light one.

quests.title: The Seal
quests.subtitle: An OR-gate, one optional task, and no rewards
description: Locked. On a canvas this dark the locked wash can afford to be gentler than on, say,
Vanilla Plus -- because the item's own colours are already standing out against the
background, so dimming it slightly is enough to say 'not yet'.
The outline of a locked node is the darkest border in any shipped theme. It is meant
to be nearly lost against the canvas, which is what 'you cannot go here' looks like.

quests.title: What the Dark Said
quests.subtitle: Two hand-ins, in order, and a long description
description: The long-description quest. This is the page to open if you want to know how a very
dark theme handles a long body of text -- and the answer is that it needs its faint
tone to be brighter than a dark theme's faint tone usually is.
On Modern, faint text is roughly half the body's brightness, which is comfortable
against a mid-grey panel. Against this canvas, half of white is too dim to read at
length, so this theme's faint tone is set higher. That is the sort of thing that only
shows up in a page of prose rather than in a label.
Scroll down for REQUIRES. The cross there is a mid purple-grey: legible, and clearly
not the green of the tick beside it.
The scrollbar is a violet thumb on a near-black track, which makes it the most
saturated scrollbar in the gallery. It is also the token pair this theme gained this
round -- before that it borrowed the raised surface and a control edge, and on a
canvas this dark that produced a track with no contrast against the panel at all.
As in every chapter, this paragraph exists to make the body taller than the clip.

tasks.title: And I did not need a torch

quests.title: The Core
quests.subtitle: Invisible until it is done
description: Hidden, in the position every chapter's last node occupies.
On this theme the gap is almost impossible to spot, because a slightly darker patch
of near-black on near-black is not much of a gap. That is worth knowing rather than
wondering about -- a hidden node is still hidden, and this is just what that looks
like on a very dark palette.

chapters.title: Amethyst
chapters.subtitle: Pale violet crystal, and the roundest theme
description: A crystal palette: the surfaces are dark but not black, and the accent is a pale violet
bright enough to be the light source rather than the surface.
This is the roundest theme in the set at a radius of 6, against Modern's 4 and Tome's 8.
Three radii, all different, all applied to the same panels -- which is what makes the
radius a parameter rather than a constant that happens to be 4.
Its locked outline is a desaturated slate violet, and its blocked word is a brighter grey
violet. As on every theme, the node recedes and the word explaining it does not.

quests.title: A Good Seam
quests.subtitle: The entry node, and the only one named
description: Pale violet on slate violet, which is the closest the gallery gets to a theme with no
hue contrast at all -- both ends of the accent range are violet, and the difference
between them is entirely brightness.
The completed colour is a green, which is the one hue in this theme that is not violet
and is there so that 'done' is unmistakable even in peripheral vision.

quests.title: Four Shards
quests.subtitle: A count, so the progress bar appears
description: The bar's fill is a pale violet and its track is a dark slate, which is a bigger gap
than most themes manage -- a consequence of the accent being the brightest thing here.
The count beside it is in the faint tone, which on this theme is a muted lilac rather
than a grey. A grey faint tone on a violet canvas reads as a colour that was forgotten.

quests.title: Chip Away
quests.subtitle: Repeatable, with a cooldown
description: A hexagon at size 40 in pale violet. On a radius-6 theme a hexagon's corners are the
flattest thing on screen, because it is the one shape whose corners are not rounded --
which makes it the shape to look at if you want to see what the radius is doing to
everything else.

quests.title: The Geode
quests.subtitle: An OR-gate, one optional task, and no rewards
description: Locked. The wash over it is a near-black violet, and the icon underneath stays
readable -- which on this theme takes some care, because a violet wash over a violet
icon can lose the item's own colours entirely.
This is the node to look at if you are deciding whether to write a theme of your own:
the wash is the value most likely to be wrong, and the one with the least margin.

quests.title: Inside the Geode
quests.subtitle: Two hand-ins, in order, and a long description
description: The long-description quest, drawn in a theme whose accent and whose faint tone are
both violet. That pairing is the thing to check here: a body of prose in which every
tone is a shade of one hue is either elegant or muddy, and which one it is depends on
whether the brightness steps are far enough apart.
Scroll to the bottom and REQUIRES appears with its tick and its cross -- the tick
green, the cross a slate violet, and the two of them the only place on the page where
two different hues meet.
The scrollbar's thumb is a saturated violet on a dark track, which is the second-most
saturated in the gallery after Obsidian's and Neon's. Since the scrollbar gained its
own two tokens this round, a theme can finally say 'my scrollbar is violet' rather
than hoping the raised surface happens to be.
As in every chapter, this paragraph exists to make the body taller than the clip, so
the scrollbar is actually drawn.

tasks.title: And I have counted the crystals

quests.title: The Cutting Room
quests.subtitle: Invisible until it is done
description: Hidden, in the position every chapter's last node occupies.
The smallest node in this chapter at size 36 with the icon at 0.9, so when it does
appear it is nearly all item and very little border.

chapters.title: Copper
chapters.subtitle: Warm metal going green
description: Copper the metal and copper the patina in one palette -- warm orange-brown surfaces with
a green doing the accent work. It is the only theme here where the answer to 'what colour
is this' is genuinely two colours.
The available colour is the green and the in-progress colour is the orange, which on this
theme means the state colours are also the material colours. That makes the progression
readable as oxidation, which is either a nice touch or a coincidence depending on how
much credit you want to give it.
Radius 4, the same as Modern's, so this chapter is the control case for the other three
radii in the gallery.

quests.title: Fresh Copper
quests.subtitle: The entry node, and the only one named
description: A green available colour on a warm brown canvas -- the two ends of copper's life in
one screen.
The title tone is a pale cream rather than a white, which is what stops a warm palette
from reading as orange text on orange. Every theme with a warm surface has to make that
adjustment somewhere, and on this one it is in the text tones.

quests.title: Smelt It Down
quests.subtitle: A count, so the progress bar appears
description: The bar's fill is the available green and its track is a dark brown. Green on brown is
a combination that appears nowhere else in the gallery, and it is either the reason to
use this theme or the reason not to.
Bars are useful in a gallery for exactly this: six pixels of a saturated colour on a
desaturated surface is a pairing that no amount of description gets across.

quests.title: Let It Weather
quests.subtitle: Repeatable, with a cooldown
description: A hexagon at size 40 in the green. The name of this quest and its colour are the same
joke, and a hexagon is about as close as this project gets to a crystal.
The taper is a straight line rather than an arc, so at this size the six edges read
as six edges -- which on a warm palette matters more than on a cool one, because a
warm outline against a warm surface loses definition faster.

quests.title: Patina
quests.subtitle: An OR-gate, one optional task, and no rewards
description: Locked. The wash here is a warm near-black brown, and the locked outline is a very
dark brown -- which on this theme is the darkest value anywhere, darker than the
blocked word beside a quest.
That relationship holds on all fifteen themes and it is worth seeing on one where the
difference is large: a node you cannot click is quieter than the word telling you so.

quests.title: The Verdigris Log
quests.subtitle: Two hand-ins, in order, and a long description
description: The long-description quest. This is the page to read if you want to see how a warm
palette handles a long body of text, and the short answer is that it needs a cream
rather than a white.
Body text at pure white on a warm brown surface is uncomfortable to read at length --
a known property of warm backgrounds rather than a flaw in this theme -- so the body
tone here is pulled slightly towards yellow. It is the kind of adjustment that is
invisible in a label and obvious in a paragraph.
Scroll down and REQUIRES appears: a green tick and a brown cross, in the same two
colours the states use everywhere else on this canvas.
The scrollbar is a mid brown on a darker one, so it is the quietest scrollbar in the
gallery. Compare it with Neon's, where the same two tokens are a magenta on near-black
and can afford to be the loudest thing on the screen.
As in every chapter, this paragraph exists to make the body taller than the clip.

quests.title: The Lightning Rod
quests.subtitle: Invisible until it is done
description: Hidden, in the position every chapter's last node occupies. On a warm palette the
node will be the only green thing on a brown canvas when it appears, so it is easier
to spot here than on most.

chapters.title: Redstone
chapters.subtitle: Dark slate and saturated red
description: Slate surfaces with a saturated red doing all the signalling, so progression reads as
current through a wire -- which is the one idea this theme is built around, and it is
carried entirely by the connector lines and the state colours agreeing.
The available colour is a bright red and the completed colour is a green, which is the
largest hue jump between two adjacent states in the gallery. A partially-completed
chapter on this theme has both colours on screen at once.
The in-progress colour is an amber, so all four states are distinguishable at a glance
without any of them being a shade of another.

quests.title: Power On
quests.subtitle: The entry node, and the only one named
description: A bright red available colour on a dark red-brown slate. The connector line leaving
this node is the mid red, and it is the value that has to sit between the surface and
the node or the graph reads as disconnected boxes.
The title is a warm off-white rather than pure white, for the same reason Copper's is
-- a saturated warm accent beside a neutral white makes the white look blue.

quests.title: Sixteen Signals
quests.subtitle: A count, so the progress bar appears
description: The bar's fill is the red, and against a dark slate track it is the brightest thing
in the row by a wide margin.
This is the theme where the progress bar is most obviously a signal-strength meter,
which is either the intended reading or a happy accident depending on how you feel
about redstone.

quests.title: Clock Circuit
quests.subtitle: Repeatable, with a cooldown
description: A hexagon at size 40 in red. A red hexagon on dark slate is the closest the gallery
gets to a stop sign, which is a coincidence of shape and colour rather than a design
decision -- but a repeatable quest in a bright red outline does read as 'this comes
round again', which is the right reading.

quests.title: No Signal
quests.subtitle: An OR-gate, one optional task, and no rewards
description: Locked. The wash here is a dark maroon-black, and the locked outline is a very dark
red -- which is the one theme in the gallery where a locked node's border shares a hue
with the available one.
They are far enough apart in brightness to be unmistakable, and that is the property
that matters: a theme may reuse a hue for a locked state as long as it does not reuse
a brightness.

quests.title: The Schematic
quests.subtitle: Two hand-ins, in order, and a long description
description: The long-description quest, and the one to read if you want to know whether a red
accent is a problem in a body of text. It is not, and the reason is that the accent
is used for section rules and the counts rather than for the prose.
That is a general point worth taking from this chapter: a theme that wants a loud
accent has to decide where the accent is allowed, and if it is allowed in the body
text the page becomes unreadable very quickly. Modern solves it by making the accent
rare; this theme solves it by keeping the accent out of the body entirely.
Scroll down for REQUIRES: a green tick and a dim red cross, which on this palette is
the only green in the body.
The scrollbar's thumb is a mid red on a dark track, so it is legible without being
loud -- which is what a scrollbar should be, and is a decision this pair of tokens did
not have when it was borrowing the raised surface and a control edge.
As in every chapter, this paragraph exists to make the body taller than the clip.

quests.title: Full Power
quests.subtitle: Invisible until it is done
description: Hidden, in the position every chapter's last node occupies.

chapters.title: Nether
chapters.subtitle: Blood red, basalt grey and lava orange
description: The hottest palette in the set. The surfaces are dark red-brown rather than black, so
there is no neutral ground anywhere on the canvas -- everything is either red, orange
or a grey pressed up against them.
The available colour is an orange and the in-progress colour is a yellow, which are the
two closest states in the gallery. Telling them apart is possible but it takes a moment,
and that is a genuine trade this palette makes rather than a mistake: the whole theme is
built on a narrow range of hues and it buys a mood with that narrowness.
Worth comparing against Nether's opposite, End, which makes the same trade in purple.

quests.title: Through the Portal
quests.subtitle: The entry node, and the only one named
description: Orange on dark red-brown, with a lava-coloured connector leaving the node. On this
canvas the connector lines are almost as bright as the nodes, which is the one place
this theme is harder to read than a neutral one.
The hover ring follows the shape as everywhere -- on a circle it is a ring, and a pale
orange one at half alpha against this surface is among the more visible rings in the
gallery.

quests.title: Three Ingots
quests.subtitle: A count, so the progress bar appears
description: The bar's fill is the orange and its track is a very dark red. Orange on dark red is
a low-contrast pairing by the standards of most themes here, and it is the clearest
case in the gallery of a theme choosing a mood over a contrast ratio.

quests.title: Keep Digging
quests.subtitle: Repeatable, with a cooldown
description: A hexagon at size 40 in orange. At this size on this surface the six edges are still
legible, which is worth checking -- a warm outline on a warm surface is the pairing
most likely to lose its silhouette.

quests.title: Bastion Gate
quests.subtitle: An OR-gate, one optional task, and no rewards
description: Locked. The wash is a near-black red and the outline is a dark red-brown, which on
this canvas is very nearly the surface colour -- a locked node here is close to
invisible, and that is the intended reading.
The blocked word beside a quest stays clearly readable, which is the pair that always
has to differ. A node recedes; the reason it receded does not.

quests.title: What the Piglins Said
quests.subtitle: Two hand-ins, in order, and a long description
description: The long-description quest. This is the page to read if you want to judge whether a
warm, high-saturation palette can carry prose, and the honest answer is: better than
you would expect, because the body tone here is a pale sand rather than a white.
A pure white on this surface glares. Every warm theme in the set pulls its body tone
off white by some amount, and this one pulls it furthest -- towards a warm cream that
reads almost as parchment on the dark red.
Scroll down for REQUIRES: a yellow-green tick and a muted brown cross.
The scrollbar's thumb is a mid red on a dark track, so it disappears into the panel
more than most. That is a defensible choice for a theme this committed to one hue, and
a bad one if you scroll a lot -- which is exactly the sort of judgement a theme should
leave to the person choosing it rather than making on their behalf.
As in every chapter, this paragraph exists to make the body taller than the clip.

quests.title: The Crown
quests.subtitle: Invisible until it is done
description: Hidden, in the position every chapter's last node occupies.

chapters.title: End
chapters.subtitle: Void purple, darker than anything else here
description: The darkest surfaces in the gallery -- deeper than Obsidian's, which is the other
near-black theme -- with a violet accent and a pale chorus green for the completed state.
Radius 8, the same as Tome's. Tome rounds light-on-warm and this rounds dark-on-dark,
which is worth seeing side by side because the same radius on the same panel reads as a
softer edge in one and a harder one in the other.
Its progress line is a bright violet, and on a canvas this dark a line that bright reads
as a beam rather than a connector. That is the intended reading: the End's version of
progression is something travelling.

quests.title: The Gate
quests.subtitle: The entry node, and the only one named
description: A pale violet on a void purple so dark it is nearly black. The connector leaving this
node is the brightest line in the gallery, which is the single most distinctive thing
about this theme on a canvas.
The title tone is a very pale lilac rather than a white -- on a surface this dark, a
pure white would be the loudest thing on the screen rather than the node.

quests.title: Twelve Pearls
quests.subtitle: A count, so the progress bar appears
description: The bar's fill is the violet and its track is a very dark purple, so the filled part
is the only thing in the row that is visibly present.
On this theme an empty track is nearly indistinguishable from the panel behind it,
which is the deliberate trade: an empty progress bar is not information, and the
space is better spent on the count.

quests.title: Void Fishing
quests.subtitle: Repeatable, with a cooldown
description: A hexagon at size 40 in pale violet on near-black. This is the sharpest a hexagon gets
in the gallery after High Contrast's, because the outline is bright and the field
behind it is nothing.

quests.title: The Inner Ring
quests.subtitle: An OR-gate, one optional task, and no rewards
description: Locked. The wash is a near-black violet and the outline is a dark desaturated violet,
so on this canvas a locked node is very close to invisible -- which as on Obsidian is
the intended reading rather than a mistake.
The dim wash is what does the work of saying 'not yet' here, because the outline has
nowhere to go: there is no darker value left below it.

quests.title: The Obsidian Pillar
quests.subtitle: Two hand-ins, in order, and a long description
description: The long-description quest, and the page where this theme's faint tone is doing the
most work -- because on a surface this dark, a faint tone set by the usual rule would
be invisible.
Body text is a light lavender and the faint tone is a mid one, and the gap between
them is wider than Modern's. Both of them would be called 'bright' on a dark theme in
the abstract; what matters is the step between them, not the values.
Scroll down for REQUIRES: a pale green tick and a muted violet cross. The green is the
only non-violet hue in the chapter, which makes the completed state unmistakable.
The scrollbar's thumb is a saturated violet on a very dark track -- among the loudest
in the gallery, and the pair that most obviously needed its own tokens. Before this
round the track was the raised surface, which on this theme is barely above black, so
the track was invisible and the thumb had nothing to read against.
As in every chapter, this paragraph exists to make the body taller than the clip.

quests.title: The Void
quests.subtitle: Invisible until it is done
description: Hidden, in the position every chapter's last node occupies. As on Obsidian, the gap
is almost invisible on a palette this dark -- there is not much difference between a
hole and the thing around it.

chapters.title: Deep Dark
chapters.subtitle: Almost no light, and one glow
description: The quietest theme in the set. Surfaces are barely above black and the accent is a sculk
cyan that is the only thing on the canvas with any light in it.
It is the opposite approach to Neon, which is also near-black but loud: this one has
almost no saturation anywhere except the accent, and Neon has almost nothing but.
Comparing those two chapters is the quickest way to see what a theme is actually
deciding.
Radius 2, so it is among the squarest themes -- between Vanilla Plus's 0 and Amethyst's
6. Compare the quest overlay's panel against Tome's while you are here.

quests.title: Wake Up
quests.subtitle: The entry node, and the only one named
description: A sculk cyan available colour on near-black, which is the only glow on the canvas and
therefore the only thing your eye lands on.
The hover ring is a pale cyan at half alpha, which against this surface reads as a
louder highlight than the same alpha does on any other theme -- there is so little
else competing with it.

quests.title: Nine Veins
quests.subtitle: A count, so the progress bar appears
description: The bar's fill is the cyan and its track is a near-black teal, so the filled portion
is a thin bright line and the empty portion is essentially the panel.
This is the theme where the progress bar most resembles a signal indicator, and where
the count beside it matters most -- because the bar alone does not say how far along
it is against a track you cannot see.

quests.title: Spread
quests.subtitle: Repeatable, with a cooldown
description: A hexagon at size 40 in cyan. On this theme the outline is very nearly the only line
on the canvas, so the six edges are unusually clear -- there is no surface detail
behind them to compete.
A square theme's hexagon and a rounded theme's hexagon are the same six edges. What
differs is everything around them.

quests.title: The Sensor
quests.subtitle: An OR-gate, one optional task, and no rewards
description: Locked. The wash is the most opaque in the gallery at four-fifths black, and the
locked outline is a very dark teal -- which on this canvas is one step above the
surface.
That is deliberate rather than a limitation: on a theme whose whole idea is that
there is almost no light, a locked node should be nearly unlit, and the item under
the wash carries the recognition.

tasks.title: I did not make a sound

quests.title: The City Below
quests.subtitle: Two hand-ins, in order, and a long description
description: The long-description quest. This is the page to open if you want to know whether a
theme this dark is actually usable for reading, and the answer depends entirely on
the faint tone.
A theme at this brightness has roughly a third of the range between black and white to
work with, compared with a mid-grey theme. Everything it needs to say -- body, faint,
heading, border -- has to fit into that third, and the only way to do it is to keep
the number of distinct tones small and the steps between them wide.
Scroll down for REQUIRES: a pale green tick and a dark teal cross, with the tick
again the only non-cyan hue in the chapter.
The scrollbar is a dark teal on a very dark track, and it is the quietest pair in the
gallery apart from Copper's. On a theme that has deliberately given up most of its
contrast range, that is consistent rather than wrong -- and it is the kind of value a
theme author should be choosing knowingly.
As in every chapter, this paragraph exists to make the body taller than the clip.

quests.title: The Heart
quests.subtitle: Invisible until it is done
description: Hidden, in the position every chapter's last node occupies.
When it appears it will be the brightest thing in this chapter by a wide margin -- a
pale cyan node on a canvas of near-black.

chapters.title: Terminal
chapters.subtitle: Green on black, and nothing in the way
description: Monospace green on black, which is the least Minecraft-looking theme in the set and is
here for packs that want that. Every surface in it does nothing but hold text up.
It is the second theme with a non-zero but very short motion -- 60ms on a linear curve,
against Modern's 140ms eased. Clicking between this chapter and Modern is the quickest
way to feel the difference between an eased transition and a linear one: the linear one
arrives faster and stops harder.
Radius 0, like Vanilla Plus, so the panels are square. It is the only theme that is both
square and animated.

quests.title: boot
quests.subtitle: The entry node, and the only one named
description: A bright green available colour on pure black. The connector leaving this node is the
same green at a lower brightness, which on this palette is the only way a line can be
distinguished from the node it comes from.
The title is a green-tinted white rather than a pure white. On a palette that is this
committed to one hue, a neutral white reads as a foreign colour.

quests.title: mount /dev/redstone
quests.subtitle: A count, so the progress bar appears
description: The bar's fill is the green and its track is a very dark green, so a filled bar is a
green line on black and an empty one is nothing.
This is the theme where the count beside the bar is doing the most work, because the
empty part of the track is not visible at all -- you cannot estimate the fraction, so
the number has to tell you.

quests.title: cron --every 2m
quests.subtitle: Repeatable, with a cooldown
description: A hexagon at size 40 in green. A green outline on black at this weight is the highest
contrast of any shape in the gallery at the same size -- the shape is essentially a
drawing of itself rather than a container.
Its motion is 60ms linear, so clicking into this chapter and then moving the pointer
across the sidebar feels noticeably faster than on the eased themes.

quests.title: permission denied
quests.subtitle: An OR-gate, one optional task, and no rewards
description: Locked. The wash is pure black at three-quarters, and the outline is a very dark
green -- so on this theme a locked node is a dim green box around a dimmed item, with
nothing else on the canvas.
The name of this quest is doing something the other chapters' are not: it is the
state the node is in, written on the node. That is not a theme property at all, which
is exactly why it is worth noticing here -- a quest's title is content, and a theme
cannot change it.

quests.title: man tasked
quests.subtitle: Two hand-ins, in order, and a long description
description: The long-description quest, and on a green-on-black palette a page of prose is what
the theme was designed for, which is worth saying plainly because it is the opposite
of what you would expect from the least Minecraft-looking theme in the set.
The section headings are the brightest green and the body is a mid one, so on this
chapter TASKS and REWARDS are more prominent than the text under them -- the reverse
of every other theme. That is a real trade and it is visible here and nowhere else.
Scroll down for REQUIRES: a green tick and a grey-green cross. All four states in
this theme are greens of different brightness, with the one exception of the
in-progress amber, which is the only colour on the canvas that is not green.
The scrollbar's thumb is a mid green on a very dark track, which on this canvas is
unmistakable. Compare it with Copper's, where the same two tokens are deliberately
quiet: the scrollbar tokens exist precisely so that a theme can make that choice
rather than inheriting one.
As in every chapter, this paragraph exists to make the body taller than the clip.

quests.title: exit 0
quests.subtitle: Invisible until it is done
description: Hidden, in the position every chapter's last node occupies. On this canvas the gap
is invisible until it is not, which is the one place a terminal palette and a void
palette behave identically.

chapters.title: Neon
chapters.subtitle: Near-black with magenta and cyan
description: The loudest theme in the set, and the other end of the range from Deep Dark: both are
near-black, and one of them has almost no saturation anywhere while this one has almost
nothing but.
It is also the only theme where the three visible states are three different hues -- cyan
for available, magenta for in progress, green for complete. Every other theme keeps at
least two of them in one family, and this one deliberately does not, because the whole
point of the palette is that everything glows a different colour.
Radius 6, the same as Amethyst's, so this is rounder than Modern and less round than Tome
and End.
If a theme is going to break something, this is the one that finds it: a value borrowed
from another job, an assumption about two colours being related, a shadow drawn in a
fixed colour -- all of them are visible here and invisible on a neutral palette.

quests.title: Jack In
quests.subtitle: The entry node, and the only one named
description: A cyan available colour on near-black violet, with a magenta hover ring. Three
different hues are already on screen before you have clicked anything, which is the
point.
The hover ring is the theme's magenta at half alpha, and on this canvas it is a glow
rather than a highlight -- the ring is by some margin the most visible one in the
gallery.

quests.title: Charge Up
quests.subtitle: A count, so the progress bar appears
description: The bar's fill is the cyan and its track is a very dark violet, so a filled bar is a
bright cyan strip on near-black.
If you press Submit on this quest while it is incomplete, note the held state -- the
press colour is a magenta, so the same control passes through three hues in one
interaction. That is legal, and on most themes it would look like a bug.

quests.title: Re-Sync
quests.subtitle: Repeatable, with a cooldown
description: A hexagon at size 40 in cyan on near-black violet. High contrast and this theme are
the two that make a hexagon look sharpest, for opposite reasons: one has a white
outline and one has a bright hue against nothing.
The six edges are a good place to check that a shape's outline uses the border token
and not the fill -- on a theme with this much saturation, a node fill showing through
would be immediately obvious.

quests.title: Offline
quests.subtitle: An OR-gate, one optional task, and no rewards
description: Locked. The wash is a near-black at roughly two-thirds, and the locked outline is a
dark violet -- so a locked node here still has a faintly visible border, which on
this palette is a deliberate choice: a theme this saturated looks broken if something
is invisible.
The blocked word beside a quest is a grey violet rather than a vivid one. A dim state
should not be using the loudest colour in the palette, even as a word.

quests.title: Packet Capture
quests.subtitle: Two hand-ins, in order, and a long description
description: The long-description quest, and the hardest page in the gallery to make readable --
which makes it the most useful one to look at. Three saturated hues on one screen is
a design that is either striking or a headache, and a long body of text is where that
gets settled.
The body tone here is a pale lavender rather than a white, and the faint tone is a
muted violet. Neither of them is saturated at all, and that is the trick: the hues
are for the states and the headings, and the prose is deliberately colourless so
that the colour means something.
Scroll down for REQUIRES: a cyan tick and a grey violet cross, which is the pairing
this theme repeats in a dozen places. The cross is never vivid on any theme -- an
unmet prerequisite is not an error, and colouring it like one would be a lie about
the state of the quest.
The scrollbar is a magenta on near-black, and it is the loudest scrollbar in the
gallery. Compare it with Copper's, which is the quietest: both are a defensible
answer to the same question, and the pair of tokens exists so that a theme can choose
rather than inherit.
As in every chapter, this paragraph exists to make the body taller than the clip, so
the scrollbar is actually drawn in this palette.

quests.title: Ghost in the Machine
quests.subtitle: Invisible until it is done
description: Hidden, in the position every chapter's last node occupies.
Fifteen chapters, fifteen themes, and this is the end of the gallery. If two of them
looked identical anywhere in the middle of it, something is wrong -- every theme in
this file resolves to forty-one distinct colours, and a test asserts that none of
them shares a name or a label with another.
